advisor.summary: A cross-tested profit-sharing design under Reg. §1.401(a)(4)-8: allocation classes replace the uniform percentage of pay, and nondiscrimination is tested on the benefit each allocation projects to at retirement rather than on the contribution itself. Because a dollar allocated to a 55-year-old owner has far less time to compound than a dollar allocated to a 30-year-old employee, the owner can take an allocation approaching the §415(c) ceiling while staff receive the gateway minimum — typically 5% of pay. With the right demographics, 85–90% of total plan dollars land in the owner's account and the staff cost is fully deductible. The engine caps the modeled owner allocation at 25% of owner wages (or 20% of self-employment earnings) and the §415(c) limit; it does not model the required staff gateway cost, which must be priced from the census before anything is promised.
mechanics: Participants are grouped into allocation classes — owner, managers, staff, or even one class per person — and each class receives its own contribution rate, set fresh every year.

Cross-testing under Reg. §1.401(a)(4)-8 converts allocations into equivalent benefit accrual rates at testing age; the plan satisfies §401(a)(4) if projected benefits, not contributions, are nondiscriminatory — the age-leverage engine of the design.

The gateway is the price of admission: before cross-testing is permitted, each NHCE must receive the lesser of 5% of compensation or one-third of the highest HCE allocation rate — budget roughly 5% of staff pay in every year the owner is funded.

The owner's allocation is bounded by §415(c) annual additions — $72,000 for 2026, counting deferrals and all employer money — on compensation up to the §401(a)(17) cap of $360,000, and the employer's aggregate deduction by §404(a)(3) at 25% of eligible payroll.

The engine caps the modeled owner allocation at 25% of owner W-2 wages (or 20% of self-employment earnings) and the §415(c) limit, and does not model the staff gateway cost — the TPA's census-priced illustration supplies the true net numbers.

The design is usually bolted onto a 401(k): deferral plus safe harbor nonelective plus new comparability is the standard small-plan owner-max stack, and the chassis a cash balance plan can later stack on.

authority.note: Cross-testing: allocations tested as equivalent benefits, plus the minimum-allocation gateway for new comparability designs.
The underlying nondiscrimination requirement the benefits-basis testing satisfies.
The per-participant annual-additions cap — $72,000 for 2026, inclusive of deferrals and all employer contributions.
The employer deduction limit — 25% of aggregate participant compensation; rarely binding in owner-weighted designs but always checked.
Caps compensation counted per participant at $360,000 for 2026.
The 2026 COLA figures for the §415(c) and §401(a)(17) limits used in this record.

requirements: A TPA-administered plan document with class-based allocation language and annual cross-testing.
Favorable demographics — the owner meaningfully older than the average employee; the design lives on that age gap.
Cash flow to fund the staff gateway in every year the owner takes an allocation.
A clean, on-time annual census: ages, hire dates, compensation, and ownership.
risks: Demographic drift is the recurring failure mode: hiring an older employee or losing a key young one can flip a passing design to failing — testing is annual, not set-and-forget.
The gateway is unconditional once cross-testing is used: funding the owner while skipping the staff contribution in a tight year is a qualification failure requiring correction.
§415(c) counts all annual additions — deferrals and safe harbor money shrink the owner's profit-sharing headroom well below the raw $72,000.
Cross-tested plans with extreme allocations draw IRS attention — use a reputable TPA and keep the annual testing file.
Late or sloppy census data produces failed tests discovered after funding; corrections under the EPCRS framework (Rev. Proc. 2021-30) are expensive.
stateNotes: Employer contributions are deductible wherever the state conforms to federal taxable income or starts from federal AGI — the common case; confirm treatment in non-conformity states in the client's footprint.
PTET interaction: both the staff gateway and the owner allocation reduce pass-through income before a PTET election is computed, so PTET estimates should be re-run once the design study lands.
Missouri conforms through RSMo §143.121, and for Missouri SALT Parity Act electors (RSMo §143.436) the contributions reduce the PTET base as well.
reviewChecklist: Current-year TPA design study in the file showing the owner/staff dollar split on real census data.
Cross-testing run on final census before the owner's allocation is fully funded.
Owner's §415(c) headroom computed net of deferrals and safe harbor money — the modeled amount does not exceed it.
Gateway funding for every eligible NHCE confirmed and budgeted.
Modeled input matches the design study, and the staff cost is presented to the client separately — the engine does not net it.

client.teaser: Give your team a fair, set amount — and point most plan dollars at your own retirement.
client.headline: A retirement plan design that puts most of the dollars in your account
plainEnglish: Most company plans give everyone the same percent of pay. The law also allows a smarter design. It rests on a simple fact: a dollar saved at 55 has ten years to grow, but a dollar saved at 30 has thirty-five.

Because of that, an older owner may take a much larger share today. Your employees get a solid, fully deductible amount — usually five percent of pay. The design sends the large remainder to you, often up to the legal cap of $72,000 a year.
Your team still sees a real benefit, which helps you hire and keep good people. A plan specialist tests the design each year to keep it inside the rules.
client.analogy: Two people must fill the same size tank by the same deadline. The one who starts later gets the wider hose. This design hands the wider hose to you.
benefits: Direct up to $72,000 a year (2026) into your own account
With the right team mix, most plan dollars land with the owner
Staff amounts are a visible benefit and fully deductible
Amounts can change every year — bigger in good years, smaller in tight ones
steps: WE gather your employee roster and have a specialist design the split.
YOU see the exact owner-versus-team dollar split before committing.
WE set up or amend the plan and calendar the funding deadlines.
YOU send the yearly employee census on time so the testing stays clean.
clientCommitments: Fund the required staff amount in any year you fund your own
Send accurate employee data — ages, pay, hire dates — on time each year
Expect the split to shift as your team ages or turns over

annualMaintenance: Annual census collection and cross-testing before owner funding
Allocation resolutions, funding by the return deadline, and Form 5500 filing
Design re-check as demographics shift, with the cash balance upgrade priced when profits support it
deliverables: TPA design study with the owner/staff dollar split
Plan document or amendment with class-based allocation language
Annual testing results and funding confirmation for the file
